items.title: Buckingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2019
items.q: They certainly didn’t come from affluent backgrounds nor did James Brown.

ctx.x: Good answer. I’m not sure I can verbalize this question, but sometimes I read sociologists writing about music and then you read musicians talking about where their music came from. And a lot of times they’re not sort of on the same page. I wonder how much you feel the social conditions that musicians grow up in affects their musicianship.

Good question. Well if you look at the greats, the legends, they certainly didn’t come from affluent background. Louis Armstrong certainly didn’t. Hank Williams certainly didn’t. I think you go to any great legendary musician and it usually comes — I mean Dolly, very humble backgrounds. You’re talking about I mean really humble backgrounds, and a lot of these people, whether it’s country, blues, jazz, rock & roll, Elvis certainly didn’t come from an affluent background. He was influenced by Chuck Berry and Fats…

least this is the way it used to be. Now, somebody told me today, one of the students said something to me about — I was talking about the recording and how it used to be, the studios. A student said, “Yeah but it might be more democratized now because everybody can make a record.” And I said, “You’re right. Everybody who has a laptop can put on garage band and make a record. items.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: James Brown had his big 18 piece band and they were like a machine.

ctx.x: I taught a course at Vanderbilt for eight years, it’s called Rhythm & Blues Tore Down the Walls of Segregation. I’m teaching it now at Virginia/Wesleyan in Virginia Beach where

I live now. I taught it at Vanderbilt for eight years. But yeah, very passionate about that. Because I lived through it in the 60s. My band in Richmond, we became a really popular back-up band for black artists. Back then there were very few artists that carried bands. James Brown had his big 18 piece band and they were like a machine. I get chills just thinking about that, when I first saw that 18 piece, that curtain open up and those guys are in tuxedos.
